mappings.note: IST as GMT+5:30 is read straight off India's standard meridian at 82.5 E, so it is longitude identification for India. Not LO-3, which is about India's physical features rather than its meridian.
Why one standard time replaces many local times - the premise is that longitude makes local time vary across a country, which is LO-2. Not LO-1: no compass direction is at issue.
Crossing the Date Line eastward: the line is the 180 meridian (LO-2) and what changes is the calendar day (C-SST1.1-LO-3). Distinct from the westward item only in direction, so it shares the pair.

Why the Date Line zigzags off 180 degrees - a fact about the meridian's drawn course, hence LO-2. C-SST1.1-LO-3 is not cited because no day/night mechanism is tested, only the line's political routing.

Asks which map component is wrongly described across scale, direction arrow, symbols and title - the map-furniture set named in LO-4. Not the competency, since LO-4 covers scale, direction and symbols together.
Fill-in for the torrid zone around the Equator; the zone is identified from its latitude band. Not C-SST1.1-LO-2, whose zones are the earth's spheres rather than heat belts.
Assertion-reason on the globe being more faithful than a flat map - a projection point with no matching outcome, so held at competency level.

Why longitude-based local time is awkward in a wide country; the reasoning runs off the east-west spread of meridians, so LO-2. Not LO-3, which concerns physical features and not the country's longitudinal width as a time problem.
Requires matching each heat zone to its latitude band and spotting the mismatch - a latitude-reading task. Grouped with the other zone items because the frame offers only LO-2 for them.

Multi-statement item on IST relative to GMT and on time running later eastward; both are longitude facts. Not C-SST1.1-LO-3, since no demonstration of day and night is required, only the meridian arithmetic.
The legend as the key to conventional symbols, which is LO-4's symbol clause. Distinct from the scale items but under the same outcome, which is the only one naming map symbols.
One-line definition of a map. Competency level because LO-4 requires a map to be drawn with scale, direction and symbols, which this does not ask.
Names scale as the map-to-ground ratio - the scale element of LO-4, stated as a definition rather than applied.
Recall of the four cardinal directions, the bare form of locating directions on a flat surface. Not LO-4, no map is being constructed.
The N arrow as the north indicator; an orientation device, so LO-1 rather than LO-4's feature symbols.
Definition of a globe. LO-2 names the globe only as the surface for reading latitudes, which is not what this asks, so the competency is the honest altitude.
The Equator's value of 0 degrees - the baseline of the latitude grid named in LO-2.
Names the parallels of latitude as the east-west imaginary lines. Not LO-1, whose directions are compass bearings and not lines on the globe.
The North Pole's latitude of 90 N; LO-2 lists the poles among the things to be identified on a globe.
Explains what a scale is for, in prose rather than by calculation - still the scale element of LO-4, which is the only outcome naming it.
Globe versus flat map for faithfulness of features, distances and directions. No outcome covers projection fidelity, so the competency is cited rather than a forced LO-2.
Grid lines as the intersection of parallels and meridians used to pinpoint a place - exactly the latitude-and-longitude identification of LO-2, unlike the neighbouring globe-versus-map items.
Westward crossing of the Date Line adds a day: the meridian is LO-2 and the day change is C-SST1.1-LO-3. Not LO-4, the line is not a conventional symbol.
The distortion problem of flattening a sphere and how a globe avoids it. Competency level, as with the orange-peel item, because no outcome addresses projection.

Ujjayini's madhya rekha is cited as India's contribution to astronomy, which C-SST4.2-LO-2 names outright; C-SST1.2-LO-2 is added for the prime-meridian and longitude content. This is the one item in the chapter that reaches outside CG-SST1.

Purpose and necessity of the Date Line, which combines the 180 meridian (LO-2) with the accumulation of time differences as the earth turns (C-SST1.1-LO-3). Broader than the two crossing items, but the same two outcomes are all that fit.
Two-way conversion of 60 E and 30 W into local times: longitude values (LO-2) plus the 15-degrees-per-hour rotation rule (C-SST1.1-LO-3). Not LO-4, no scale or symbol work.

Asks both for the zones by their latitude bands (LO-2) and for the CAUSE, the varying angle of sunlight on a curved earth, which is the sun-earth relation behind C-SST1.1-LO-3. The short zone-naming items get LO-2 alone because they stop short of the cause.
